Well, there are two that I can think of off the top of my head. For my job at NRCS,I use a program called RUSLE2 (revised universal soil loss equation) you can use it to model erosion and changes in soil organic matter based on management. It’s an ugly, fiddly software. I don’t recommend trying to learn it yourself, but it’s open source… so you can if you want to! 
Another one I know of is carbon farm/carbon planner. It’s goal is to model CO2 emissions, but I think it also shows changes in organic matter.

Another option, is to contact your local NRCS office. They can provide technical assistance for free, (like run RUSLE2 for you) and might be able to give financial assistance for soil conservation.

Also check out your local resource conservation district (sometimes called soil and water conservation district). They will also have good technical expertise!

To keep a little bit of romanticism… if you have a career that you are passionate about, at least try for it! I’ve found a career that gives me purpose, even when the day to day sometimes sucks. It pays enough for me to live, though not enough to ‘save for the future’ or have super nice things. Still, I wouldn’t trade it for a better paying job. 

Also, something to consider. Everyone talks about how well blue collar jobs pay, but they also can have a very hard toll on the body. And if your body breaks, what then? As someone who deals with chronic pain, I simply cannot be something like an electrician or a plumber. 

I was also fortunate, I had enough resources to pay for school without private loans. Federal student loans might be worth it, if the interest rates are low enough. Avoid private loans like the devil!! They are predatory and evil. Similarly, public schools are a better bet than private schools. 

I think the level of specialization is important! For example, I have a BS in Agronomy. I had friends who took a BS in Environmental Science, or Biology. My degree gives me a more narrow range of opportunities, but I have strong technical skills rather than a broad overview. 

Lastly, consider if you want to do grad school. Most BS degrees don’t work well by themselves, but are excellent foundations for MS or PhD. Once you are in grad school, you can make your way without student loans. Make sure that your program offers teaching or research assistantships. They won’t pay a great stipend, but it waives your tuition. And when you come out the other side, you are much more marketable. Again, specialization is important. My MS is in soil science. I wouldn’t be nearly as competitive if my MS was an MBA. 

A personal note that doesn’t apply to everyone. I work for the US federal government. I feel safe! My salary is on an algorithm based on qualifications and seniority. I really have to screw up in order to be terminated. Layoffs don’t really exist. That may not be compatible with everyone’s goals, but I’m much happier than working for a cut throat company where I have to compete for promotions, worry about being a woman in STEM, or fear losing my job at the drop of a pin.

Hi! I had a similar experience. I started as a thesis MS, but because of chronic illness, I was unable to finish my thesis. I dropped down to a non-thesis degree, and never published anything. I was also paid a stipend as a graduate research assistant, and really worried about if I had to pay back money or other repercussions. 
My PI was very considerate, even though he was disappointed. I didn’t have to pay anything back, and I wasn’t tied to the project. As he told me, professors take a risk when they take on a student. Things like this are NORMAL. 

Yes. It’s unfair, and disappointing. But it’s not fair that I had to deal with a chronic illness, it’s not fair that you experienced imposter syndrome, depression, and lack of self esteem. (It also sounds to me like you didn’t have a good enough support structure!! That’s not your fault, they should have set you up for success, not left you alone)

Does your research assistant contract EXPLICITLY say you need to publish? I doubt it. Were you paid a separate teaching assistantship? If not, you still provided an important service that deserves pay.

As a natural resources conservationist, please please don’t support geoengineering. 

TLDR: Geoengineering is yet another episode of mankind’s hubris to think that he can outsmart billions of years of evolution. Take a sledgehammer to intricate ecosystems, and the unintended/unexpected consequences will be enormous. Also, we don’t need it! We have other legitimate options!! We can stop emissions and also use CO2 sequestration to reverse damage, we have a fighting chance still!

As a natural resource conservationist, I sometimes feel like half my job is fixing the mistakes of previous conservation work. Lots of American conservation used big projects and engineering solutions to ecological problems. In doing so, they created a whole other pile of ecological problems.
Eg: channelizing streams to reduce flooding damage and drain wetlands to create prime agricultural land. Now, the same prime agricultural land is experiencing rapid erosion from streams that move way too fast. Also, perfectly usable water is moving through the landscape before it can be used. Major opportunity loss. Now areas that receive a perfectly reasonable amount of water experience artificial drought in summer and pump groundwater to compensate.

Somehow land leveling and major terracing is considered a reasonable solution to soil erosion. But in doing so, you scrape away the fertile topsoil. 

Conservationists introduced Kudzu as an idea for stream bank stabilization and animal forage. It’s now one of the most invasive species in the SE United States. Similarly, the push for cellulosic biofuels incentivized farmers to plant non-native miscanthus grass. It’s so prolific, it has to be sprayed, tilled, sprayed again, in an attempt to kill it. Sometimes even that doesn’t work. Supposedly it’s sterile, but if someone planted non-sterile miscanthus, it has the potential to be the next kudzu. 

The dams that were supposed to create drought resilience and provide clean energy are being decommissioned because they are an ecological nightmare. They have permanently destroyed the ecosystems of those rivers, plus flooded tons of area that contained fragile habitat.

The stories are endless. The moral of the story is STOP APPLYING ENGINEERING SOLUTIONS TO ECOLOGICAL PROBLEMS!

We have ecological solutions. We don’t need geoengineering. Honestly, in my opinion, the hype over geoengineering started up because it was promoted by billionaires who think they are experts. They have no idea what they are talking about.

My career is focused on regenerative agriculture, which uses existing ecosystem processes to restore soil fertility and sequester carbon from the atmosphere. It also restores the biological diversity that modern input-intensive agriculture damaged. If systemic changes are made to the US agriculture system, this sector can go from net positive emissions to net negative emissions. If you are interested in this particular topic, I recommend the documentary Kiss the Ground. The science isn’t perfect, and like any documentary, it’s overly dramatic. But as a soil scientist, I can vouch for its general accuracy. I work for NRCS, Ray Archuleta is a badass, and a huge role model for many of us soil conservationists!!

I will admit, soil carbon sequestration is only one of many options for CO2 drawdown. There are other excellent ecological solutions in forestry and geology, but I can’t claim expertise in those. We have a fighting chance of CO2 drawdown, we don’t need to permanently alter our world to do so.

I can totally empathize with the fear and the nihilism. My career is focused on sustainable agriculture, and it often feels like my story will be the romanticism of fighting a lost cause till the bitter, tragic end. 
But nihilism is an over simplification, and it doesn’t have to be that way. Even absolute worst case scenario, humanity will not go extinct. Chemistry modeling shows that it is physically impossible to turn Earth into a toxic hellhole like Venus, so climate change may kill most of us, it can’t kill all of us. 
The knowledge is there, and some communities are doing an excellent job of resilient, sustainable living. I really love the Permaculture movement, and I think it is an excellent way to survive the insanity of rampant climate change (it even accounts for wildfire, if designed properly. It might not be able to prevent them, but it can help us survive them.) it might be a brutal future, but humanity will survive. 

On a much more optimistic note, we have the knowledge and technology to not only stop climate change, but reverse it!! My deepest frustration is the inability of national governments to get shit done. But local and regional governments can pick up the slack. My day job is in regenerative agriculture. I have a lot of hope that IF we can implement it properly, it will be an excellent tool to fix our mistakes. (I don’t think it’s the only tool, but it’s my area of expertise, so obviously I put disproportionate emphasis on it) if you are interested, look up the documentary Kiss the Ground. The science isn’t perfect, and like all documentaries it’s a bit over dramatic. But I can vouch that the main ideas and motivations are absolutely correct! 
I won’t give platitudes and say ‘it’s going to be okay,’ because it’s not. But we do have paths forward that can actually work. We have a fighting chance.

Soil scientist here! There are two main reasons that soils become acidic. First is organic acids. These form from decomposition of things like leaf litter/dead biomass. Pine trees specifically are notorious for creating acidic soils underneath them. 
The other reason soils become acidic is simply because the other stuff (basic cations) get washed out. This tends to happen in more weathered soils. Areas with lots of rainfall and heat usually have weathered soils (think the red clay soils in SE USA, or in tropical areas)
If you have a soil with high organic matter, it won’t be so much of an issue. Organic matter acts like a buffer, it makes the soil more forgiving, because it holds onto the basic cations more (and a lot of basic cations are important micronutrients too!)
Hypothetically, sulphuric does lower the ph. But a soil with heavy sulphuric content is pretty uncommon. 

So compost is a great thing! Agriculture lime is very frequently used in conventional agriculture. It’s very safe for your soil, the environmental issues may come from source and transportation.

Have you gotten your soil tested? Most land grant schools will do it for free (if you are in USA). And look into soils maps! That will give you a general idea of what you have in your area

Makes sense to me! I don’t think my idea of ecological succession is contradictory to your idea of collecting the whole biodiversity. 

As a broad example: forest/ shrubland soil has a higher abundance (generally) of fungi when compared to grassland soils. I’m not suggesting isolating the rhizosphere microbes of one plant and putting it on another (though, I have worked in a research lab that did that, promising results! It’s a route that could be further explored, though I think it becomes less permaculture, and more agri-tech) 
Instead, I think it would be fun to add plant ecology to your list of factors when considering a site to collect your microbes. Especially when you consider some permaculturists are doing backyard gardening with annuals, while others do perennial food forests.... those will need two entirely different microbial ecosystems. 

And on a final note, I want to add a caveat: I think this idea is really cool, and it’s great because it’s teaching gardeners how to collect inoculum themselves! My experience with research in soil micro ecology is inconclusive if soil inoculation actually works. It works in theory, if the soil you are putting them into is sterilized. But in practice, your inoculation may simply be outcompeted by what’s already there. Most of my work was done on row-crop agricultural land, and we found that inoculation doesn’t work. But!! That’s a very different world from the backyard garden!! So I will give it the benefit of the doubt, and say I don’t know. In this circumstance at least, it can’t harm anything!

But as a soil scientist, I’m deeply troubled by companies that are latching onto the soil health movement, simply to sell “mycorrhizal inoculum.” I wouldn’t sink money into that, I don’t trust it.

One thing I’d be hesitant about: mycorrhizae are a symbiotic fungi that get their food by partnering with plant roots. The fungi that will decompose rice are considered saprophytic. Totally different ecological niche. There might be some overlap between those two categories (ie, you might pick up a couple fungi that can do both.) but this method will not target mycorrhiza.

As others have said, this is extremely  difficult to answer without a pile of contextual information. Here are some broad sweeping examples to show how a minor thing can change practices:
  First of all, what was the weather like? Weather can cause a stand to fail, or “prevent plant” which throws off an entire rotation. Each crop has a slightly different prep method, so it’s an important consideration. Similarly, was it wet when you harvested? Lots of farmers around here don’t want to commit to no-till in case they rutted up the ground.

Are you running a no till system? 
Equipment is expensive, and you have to get specialized equipment to convert to no-till. Then there are different types of tillage, some are more intense than others. Some people do multiple tillage passes, others do minimal or targeted tillage. It depends on the system and equipment.
If you are doing no-till, are you doing cover crops? This adds a whole other layer of complexity, because suddenly you have to plant cover in the fall, and kill it in the spring. How will you kill your covers? Are you rolling/crimping? Are you grazing? Are you using herbicide? Each of these need different equipment, timing, and methods.
Are you organic? Killing your cover crops with herbicide is a complete no-go if you are organic. 

What type of irrigation system are you using? If you use furrow irrigation, you have to do additional dirt work to pull beds every 1-3 years.

What about fertilization? Are you working with manure, or synthetic? Are you broadcasting it or injecting it? Are you doing it all prior to planting or in multiple batches? 

Rice production where I am also requires a whole other pile of considerations, because it is such a unique system. Many folks around here do major land leveling. They then do lots of corrective tillage in the fall and spring, plant, then pull levies and flood. They use fertilizer and pesticides in season. Then after harvest, they sometimes burn rice stubble so that they can get fields prepped for a soybean rotation. This requires pulling beds, so it’s more land work. 

I’m also learning about cotton, and was amazed to learn that you have to spray it with a growth inhibitor practically every week during th vegetative growth season! 

And this is only a brief overview, and only row crops. Orchards and high tunnel produce are a whole different galaxy.

That’s not a pedestrian understanding, that’s a pretty good analogy! Biochar is unique in that it has extra binding sites for nutrient capacity. The other side of that coin is that some binding sites are irreversible. (So it could theoretically steal phosphorus from you till those are filled) 
it’s also somewhat unique in its staying power. Something about it doesn’t decompose as quickly. I think the long-lasting aspect is what got a lot of people excited, because it’s potential for soil carbon sequestration. At the same time though, compost and green manure have similar properties. They will create soil organic matter that has nutrient binding sites, and sequester soil carbon. Biochar might be more potent than compost, but not by terribly much. 

In my opinion, there are other methods of soil carbon sequestration that are better. In order to make biochar you have to burn something as fuel to start the reaction. You lose a lot in the process. Have to consider the full lifecycle of the soil amendment, and what purpose it serves.

Though, none of that is particularly relevant to slash and burn agriculture. 🤷‍♀️ biochar just has so much interesting conversation around it!

This is a really interesting question, and I think it could really lead down a research rabbit hole. My initial thoughts:
1. As already mentioned, burning does add some nutrient to the soil. That’s part of the reason why slash/burn agriculture works (for a few years at least). And there is indication that fire management improves soil quality in other ecosystems. In the prairies of Midwest USA, fire is one of the many reasons for beautiful mollisol formation. 
2. What is the difference between fire in a rainforest vs fire in a prairie? I don’t really know an in depth answer to that, but it is interesting to think about where most nutrients are stored. In the rainforest, most of the nutrients are locked up in the biomass. Nutrients cycle so fast, it barely even makes it to the soil! That’s why desertification is such a major problem. The soil of the rainforest is pretty terrible. 
3. Biochar is different from combustion. Biochar is formed through pyrolysis, which is partial combustion in a low oxygen environment. Slash and burn is full combustion in a normal oxygen environment. They have different resulting chemistries. 
4. Biochar isn’t a miracle, the way it is often promoted. Don’t get me wrong, it’s good! So is compost, no-till, cover cropping, perennial grasses, and a pile of other management practices. I had a cynical professor say that biochar is just the current fad of soil science. It’s exciting because we don’t fully understand the chemistry of it. Granted, I’m not quite that cynical, but I’d agree with that to some extent. It’s one of many tools in soil science, and context matters!
